name: Kasner Universe with a Magnetic Field
description: Kasner's anisotropic universe threaded by a uniform magnetic field along one axis, with no matter in it. The tension of the field pulls that axis to nothing at both ends of time, and the universe passes from one Kasner vacuum at early times to another at late times.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The magnetic field points along $z$.
history: Galaxies have magnetic fields, and in 1966 every attempt to explain how they arose after the big bang faced "difficulties which seem to be insurmountable", in Kip Thorne's words [thorne1967]. Fred Hoyle had raised one way out in 1958, a field that was there from the beginning, and by Yakov Zel'dovich's account he "considered it unsatisfactory and unpalatable" [zeldovich1965magnetic]. Zel'dovich took it up anyway in January 1965 and assumed "that a primordial homogeneous magnetic field existed in the universe" [zeldovich1965magnetic]. He put its strength "at the present time" at "less than $3 \times 10^{-9}$ G" [zeldovich1965magnetic]. Such a universe can be the same at every place, but a field has to point somewhere, and "isotropy is destroyed by the presence of a preferred direction along the field" [zeldovich1965magnetic]. How does a universe expand when one of its directions is special?¶Gerald Rosen had the simplest answer in print three years earlier [rosen1962]. Going through the symmetries that the Einstein-Maxwell equations allow, he came out with a "new solution", a space alike at every point that holds a uniform magnetic field and no matter [rosen1962, rosen1964, jacobs1969]. It is Kasner's vacuum with a field laid along one axis: at early times the three axes go as powers of the time, $t^{p_1}$, $t^{p_2}$, and $t^{p_3}$, as they do in a universe with no field [kastor2015, kasner1921]. A magnetic field pulls along its lines like a stretched band and pushes out sideways, so "the rising tension along the magnetic field lines accelerates the longitudinal collapse" of space or slows its expansion in that direction [thorne1967]. The length along the field therefore rises to a greatest value and shrinks again, and the universe ends as a second Kasner vacuum whose exponent along the field is $-p_3/(1 + 2p_3)$ [jacobs1969, kastor2015].¶Thorne cared how such a universe begins, because a field above $4.4 \times 10^{13}$ gauss puts most of its energy into pairs of electrons and positrons, and he doubted that an ordered field would come out of them [thorne1967]. A primordial field had to start finite, and that takes a universe that has expanded "by a finite amount perpendicular to the magnetic field lines" since its first instant and without limit along them [thorne1967]. He called such a beginning "pancake-like": space is squeezed flat along the field while the field lines keep their spacing, so "the magnetic field strength at the singularity is finite" [thorne1967]. His conclusion, sent off in September 1966, was that if the fields of galaxies are primordial "then the universe was probably very anisotropic in its early stages" [thorne1967]. A. G. Doroshkevich had found the same universes and drawn the same conclusions a year earlier, and Zel'dovich told Thorne so in time for a note added in proof [thorne1967, doroshkevich1966].¶Could a beginning like that still show in the sky? The microwave radiation was known in 1966 to be even to within 3 per cent around the celestial equator, and Thorne worked out that this limits the anisotropy of the universe "many orders of magnitude" more tightly than the redshifts of galaxies do [thorne1967]. Kenneth Jacobs, who had solved the same universes filled with a fluid alone, added the magnetic field at Caltech in 1968 and let all three axes differ [jacobs1968, jacobs1969]. Rosen's universe turned up among his solutions, and Thorne told him that Rosen had found it first [jacobs1969]. The pancake is the one beginning in which the field starts finite, and it needs the two axes across the field to be equal, "a subset of measure zero" of the possible beginnings [jacobs1969]. A primordial field of $10^{-9}$ to $10^{-7}$ gauss today, Jacobs concluded, "has negligible effect upon the temperature anisotropy of the cosmic microwave radiation" [jacobs1969].¶In 2015 David Kastor and Jennie Traschen took Melvin's magnetic universe, a static bundle of field lines, and continued its radius to imaginary values, which turns the radius into a time [kastor2015]. The result is Rosen's universe with the two axes across the field equal [kastor2015]. B. Kent Harrison's transformation, which makes Melvin's universe out of flat space, makes the whole of Rosen's family out of Kasner's vacuum [kastor2015, harrison1968]. The step from one set of Kasner exponents to the next is, in their words, "reminiscent of the BKL approach to a spacelike singularity", the endless run of Kasner epochs that Vladimir Belinskii, Isaak Khalatnikov, and Evgenii Lifshitz found in the vacuum [kastor2015, bkl1970]. A field along one axis makes one such step [kastor2015]. Eighteen years earlier Victor LeBlanc had found a set of Bianchi type I universes with a magnetic field and a fluid that "generates oscillations on the Kasner circle", and he conjectured that generic ones approach it toward the past [leblanc1997].¶With four years of data from the Cosmic Background Explorer, John Barrow, Pedro Ferreira, and Joseph Silk went back to the microwave sky in 1997 [barrow1997]. They worked out how a homogeneous magnetic field disturbs the radiation in the most general flat and open anisotropic universes [barrow1997]. Their upper limit on "the present strength of any primordial homogeneous magnetic field" is $3.4 \times 10^{-9}$ gauss, times a factor set by the density of the universe and its rate of expansion [barrow1997].

related.text: The universe with the field switched off. At $b = 0$ the metric is Kasner's vacuum, and with the field on it starts as one Kasner vacuum and ends as another [kastor2015].

Melvin's static bundle of field lines with its radius continued to imaginary values, which turns the radius into a time. The continuation is this universe with the two axes across the field equal, exponents $(0, 0, 1)$ [kastor2015].

Kasner's universe with the other simple content, a massless scalar field or a stiff fluid. Kenneth Jacobs solved the two together in 1969, a stiff fluid and a magnetic field in one universe [jacobs1969].
This universe is Bianchi type I, flat space with three scale factors, holding a uniform magnetic field along one of its axes [jacobs1969].

coordinates.name: Kasner's time

parameters.description: Exponent along $x$ at early times, with $p_1 + p_2 + p_3 = 1$
Exponent along $y$ at early times, with $p_1^2 + p_2^2 + p_3^2 = 1$
Exponent along $z$, the direction of the field, at early times, with $0 < p_3 \le 1$. At late times the three exponents are $(p_1 + 2p_3)/(1 + 2p_3)$, $(p_2 + 2p_3)/(1 + 2p_3)$, and $-p_3/(1 + 2p_3)$

Strength of the field, a pure number: observers at rest measure a magnetic field $B = (2bp_3c/\sqrt{G})\,t^{p_3 - 1}/(1 + b^2t^{2p_3})^2$ along $z$, in Gaussian units. At $b = 0$ the metric is Kasner's vacuum

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, with $t$ the proper time of Kasner's vacuum at $b = 0$, and evaluate the powers of $t$ with $t$ in a fixed unit of time, so they are dimensionless and the lengths sit in $x$, $y$, and $z$. Every component assumes the two conditions on the exponents. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Rosen (axisymmetric)

parameters.description: A length, which sets the field: observers at rest measure a magnetic field $B = (c^2/\sqrt{G})(1 + \cos\eta)^2/\ell$ along $z$, in Gaussian units, which is $4c^2/(\sqrt{G}\,\ell)$ at $\eta = 0$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, x, y, z)$, with Rosen's time $\eta$ a pure number, in the axisymmetric case, where the exponents of Kasner's time are $(0, 0, 1)$ and $\tan(\eta/2) = bt$ once $x$, $y$, and $z$ are rescaled. We take components in the chart $x^0 = \eta$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
